blurb: LiDAR, radar, cameras, IMUs, force-torque, tactile, encoders, and GNSS — compared on range, cost, compute burden, and how they fail.
question: How should this robot perceive the world?
title: Robot Sensors: A Practical Reference
lede: A robot only knows what its sensors tell it, and every sensor is wrong in its own characteristic way. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} sensing technologies across six classes, with range, cost, compute burden, and the failure modes that actually cause trouble in the field.

facets.label: Use
facets.tip: What the sensor mainly feeds: environment perception & mapping, ego-state & navigation, manipulation & joint control, or safety & proximity functions.

facets.label: Range
facets.tip: Useful sensing envelope: Contact · Near (<1 m) · Mid (1–30 m) · Far (30–300 m) · Global (300 m+ or worldwide). Proprioceptive sensors (IMUs, encoders) carry no range tag.

facets.label: Compute
facets.tip: Downstream processing burden to turn raw output into robot-usable information: Trivial (a register read) · Moderate (filtering, classical DSP) · Heavy (point-cloud pipelines, stereo matching) · Extreme (deep networks, learned perception stacks).

facets.label: Adoption
facets.tip: Ubiquitous = deployed by the billion or in essentially every robot · Common = standard in its niche · Emerging = shipping but young · Research = lab stage.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional unit cost at robot-relevant grades and current volumes. Sensor prices fall fast — automotive volume has repeatedly cut categories by 10× in a decade.
